target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove scheduling barriers and help many Americans vote
objection: A national holiday would not reliably provide time off for many eligible voters because federal law does not require private employers to give paid holiday leave, and many retail and service workers would still be scheduled to work.

target: AG1's implication that a national holiday would not disadvantage anyone and would broadly improve access
objection: Low-income workers are more likely to hold jobs without guaranteed paid holiday time, so the policy would disproportionately disadvantage them relative to higher-income workers.

target: AG1's assumption that an election holiday is an effective turnout reform
objection: Research indicates that having an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1's conclusion that a national holiday should be adopted instead of other reforms
objection: More reliable ways to improve voting access are changing state employer-time-off laws and implementing automatic voter registration, not making Election Day a federal holiday.

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday would not reliably provide time away from work because private employers need not grant paid leave
objection: Even without a legal requirement for paid leave, declaring Election Day a national holiday typically changes public and employer scheduling, often closing operations or reducing hours and thereby giving many workers extra non-working time or flexibility to vote.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday would disadvantage low-income workers
objection: That disadvantage is not established, because a national Election Day holiday does not remove any baseline voting opportunity and instead adds a shared scheduling buffer that low-income workers also receive.

target: AG1's argument that a national holiday would solve registration or administrative uncertainty by giving voters time on Election Day
objection: Some registration or verification problems must be resolved before Election Day, so extra time on the day itself cannot fix them.

target: AG1's assumption that holiday timing can reduce administrative uncertainty barriers
objection: On national holidays, election offices and assistance channels are often less available or staffed more lightly, so the holiday can actually make it harder to get the help needed to resolve registration or verification issues.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday does not directly address registration/admin uncertainty
objection: For many voters, the barrier is the lack of time to seek help or complete required steps during school or work hours, so giving protected time on Election Day can directly help them resolve those issues.

target: AG2's claim that election offices are less available on holidays and that this makes a holiday unreliable
objection: That reliability objection is too strong because at least some administrative barriers depend on whether voters can use election-official assistance during available hours, and a holiday can provide that time.

target: AG1's argument that Election Day as a holiday would create meaningful additional time windows for low-income workers
objection: Because private employers are not required to give paid leave and can still schedule retail and service workers on federal holidays, many low-income workers would not actually get extra time to vote.

target: AG2's claim that school and other routines shifting off the holiday still do not solve scheduling barriers
objection: The barrier is not only paid leave; it is also access to polling places and election assistance during their operating hours, and a holiday can expand or stabilize those daytime access windows.

target: AG2's claim that the policy would not reliably reduce scheduling barriers
objection: When polling and assistance are more accessible during the day, scheduling constraints stop blocking voting as often, so the holiday can reduce real access friction.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would create meaningful non-work time for low-income workers
objection: Even if schools or other routines shift, retail and service workers can still be required to work on federal holidays, so the day may not produce real non-work time for them.

target: AG1's claim that reducing school/caregiving conflicts helps low-income workers
objection: Shifting school or caregiving calendars does not remove employer-imposed work schedules, so the main barrier for many low-income workers remains.

target: AG1's combined holiday-plus-reform argument
objection: Automatic voter registration can reduce registration uncertainty, but it does not guarantee time away from work; therefore, pairing it with a holiday does not remove the holiday's unequal-access problem for low-income workers.

target: AG1's claim that holiday timing is reliable when combined with registration/admin reforms
objection: Even with registration reforms, some voters still need election-office assistance on Election Day, and reduced holiday staffing or hours can still leave those administrative barriers unresolved.

target: AG2's claim that reduced staffing on a holiday makes administrative help unavailable
objection: Polling places still operate on Election Day and can handle common voter problems at the point of voting, so reduced off-site staffing does not show that a holiday makes administrative resolution generally unreliable.

target: AG2's claim that automatic voter registration plus a holiday still leaves election-office help too limited
objection: Election Day is a planned nationwide election date, so administrations can staff polling-place operations and voter assistance for that day even if it is also a national holiday.

target: AG2's claim that holiday timing inherently makes administrative resolution unreliable
objection: That claim is not established as a general rule, because election administrations can plan for the holiday date and automatic voter registration reduces the number of people who need last-minute administrative help.
